newsitem.title: Zaire: Confusion reigns as rebels block access to Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Confusion reigns as rebels block access to Zaire.

text.p: Zairean rebels stopped U.N. agencies entering a large swathe of eastern Zaire on Friday to search for thousands of lost people while efforts to despatch an intervention force to the region flagged still further.

Complete confusion reigned over the whereabouts and number of hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and homeless Zaireans with the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR openly contradicting itself.
Field officers said reports from the UNHCR's headquarters in Geneva, based on satellite imagery, were not borne out by facts on the ground.

"We have no confirmation, no reports, and no information about any refugees moving towards Goma from Sake or the other side of Sake. We know nothing about any supposed 50,000 refugees moving toward Goma," Ray Wilkinson, UNHCR spokesman in Goma told reporters.

About 500,000 Hutu refugees fleeing fighting between the rebels and their Hutu foes poured through the eastern Zaire border town of Goma towards the end of last week, leaving an estimated 700,000 still unaccounted for.

A Reuters correspondent who visited the outskirts of Sake, some 20 kms (12 miles) west of Goma, on Friday said the only refugees he saw were a small group of about 150 outside Mugunga camp from where the bulk of last week's refugees fled.
"This road is emptier than it has been for any time over the last two years," one aid official told Reuters.
Wilkinson added that Zairean rebels, backed by Rwanda which claims the UNHCR figures are inflated, were preventing aid agencies going into the area to find out what was going on.
"We cannot leave Goma, we have been told the area outside has been declared a military zone and no international staff are being allowed outside the town," Wilkinson said.

The rebels are believed to be moving in on the remnants of Rwanda's Hutu-dominated ex-army and associated militia groups, accused of leading the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
On Thursday, the UNHCR, citing satellite photos as evidence, spoke of a group of 200,000 refugees moving north from Bukavu.

But it also said it had located 250,000 south of Bukavu, as well as 50,000 west of the Masisi region west of Goma, about 100,000 north of Sake in the Masisi plus, deeper into Zaire, and another 100,000 people in the Fizi area, some 100 km (60 miles) south of Uvira.
The confusion complicated the task of representatives from about 40 countries and aid organisations meeting at Kelly Barracks at the U.S. army base in Stuttgart, southwest Germany.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, which is coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission, told a news conference that estimates presented at the meeting of the number of refugees in need of help varied between 100,000 and 500,000.
"We're going to find out (how many there are) before we commit any troops," he said. "By the end of the weekend I would hope we will have developed a full slate of options."
"A firm commitment (to send troops) can only be made later by governments after they have considered all the options," he told a news conference.
"The mandate we have is to open a (relief) corridor to those who really need it," he said. "We're not here to feed and transport them, but to open the corridor."

The situation became even more confused after the head of a U.S. military assessment team in Rwanda said he could only be certain of one group of 150,000 to 175,000 refugees heading north from Bukavu.
Major-General Edward Smith said they seemed to be bona fide refugees. The group was between 100 and 150 km (60 and 95 miles) from Goma, but he could not say where it was heading.
"I can't speak for the U.N., but I'm confident that with the data we have and the means of getting the figures that we have an accurate estimate," he said.
Wilkinson was scathing about Smith's statement.
"As for General Smith's claims in Kigali about the number of people moving 150 km (95 miles) south of Goma, this is absurd. Has the man never looked at a map?" he said.
The direct road distance between Goma and Bukavu is less than 150 km (95 miles).
Another complicating factor for military planners is that the satellite technology cannot make distinction between types of refugees or between displaced Zaireans..
There had been no new significant arrival of refugees in Goma, aid officials there said.
The United States has scaled down its commitment to the intervention force since the 500,000 returned home and is not now planning to contribute combat troops.
